title: Mayan City-States
capsule: The Maya civilization comprised a constellation of competing city-states in southeastern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, and parts of Honduras and El Salvador, with continuous cultural development from the Preclassic period (c. 2000 BC) through the Spanish conquest completed in 1697. The Classic period (c. 250–900 AD) saw over forty cities each with populations of 5,000–50,000, dominated by rival powers such as Tikal and Calakmul whose warfare is documented by hieroglyphic stelae; the Maya developed the most sophisticated writing system in the pre-Columbian Americas along with advanced calendrical and astronomical knowledge. A 9th-century political collapse, driven by a combination of prolonged drought, warfare, and environmental degradation, depopulated the southern lowland centers, though northern cities like Chichen Itza and Uxmal flourished into the Postclassic. The dataset's attestation from 247 BC through 849 AD captures the pre-Classic emergence through the Classic florescence.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Major Classic-period city locations and rough territorial spheres of influence are reconstructed from LiDAR survey, excavation, and epigraphy; outer boundaries between polities and the full extent of any given city-state's control are interpreted from limited epigraphic and archaeological evidence, making the geometry a broad approximation.
